payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Turn the image into a drawing made from chalk
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image visibly render its surfaces with a chalk-like appearance, rather than merely adding grain or a filter to the source image?
node.criteria: Pass if, compared with the source, visible surface marks or tonal treatment make the image read as rendered with chalk. Fail if the source’s surface appearance remains or the only change is generic grain or filtering that does not produce a chalk-like rendering. Unknown only if the surface treatment cannot be observed.
node.endpoint: The drawing has visibly chalk-like surface marks or tonal treatment.
node.necessity: The instruction specifies that the drawing is made from chalk; a drawing without a visibly chalk-like rendering does not fulfill that requested material appearance.

node_traces.evidence: Compared with the source photograph, the edited image has a visibly drawn, chalk-like treatment: the giraffes and foliage have softened, sketchy outlines and mottled tonal shading, while the ground and sky show broad smudged strokes rather than photographic surface detail. This goes beyond generic grain alone.

response.content: {"text":"The node’s criterion is broadly aligned with the requested chalk material, and the trace cites visible changes beyond generic grain. However, its pass threshold may be too permissive: the edited image retains photographic detail in the giraffes and adds strong blur/noise and smearing, which could be mistaken for chalk without establishing that the image is actually rendered as a chalk drawing. Tighten the distinction between chalk-specific surface treatment and generic filtering, and assess the image as a whole against the source. The trace’s high-confidence “pass” conflicts with the aggregate “partial” reference, but that label is not atomic ground truth: investigate whether the node is treating some chalk-like marks as complete fulfillment, and calibrate confidence to the mixed evidence rather than forcing a label. Preserve an unknown outcome for genuinely unobservable treatment; there are no transport, schema, or dependency failures indicated here."}
